tagline.text: Siquijor's highest peak and the healers' herb forest at the heart of the island

location.label: Location
location.text: Central highlands of Siquijor Island (a mountain area spanning several municipalities, including Lazi, Siquijor and Larena)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~1,600 (free entry; per person per day, depending on transport)

children.text: Bandilaan Natural Park is a protected forest area around the island's highest peak (most commonly given as about 557 m) in the center of Siquijor. From the summit tower you can see the whole island and the sea toward Negros, and because this is the forest where traditional healers gather herbs, it is the closest you can get to Siquijor's mystical reputation.

Bandilaan Natural Park (often called Mt. Bandilaan National Park) is a protected forest area right in the middle of Siquijor Island. Figures vary from one guide to another, but it was declared a forest reserve in 1940 by President Manuel Quezon under Proclamation No. 523, and the area most often given is about
212 hectares

. Some sources list 244 or 271 hectares, so treat the area as a figure that differs by source. The forest also serves as the island's largest watershed. Check the latest notices for the reserve's forest condition and management rules. Recent articles report that island visitor arrivals rose from about 168,000 in 2019 to more than 270,000 in 2025, increasing the pressure on forest conservation.
The height of Mt. Bandilaan, the island's highest peak, also differs by source. Travel guides and many reports most often give
(1,827 ft), while map services and some blogs list

. Either way, it is the highest point in Siquijor. Its former name was Mt. Malabahok, and a 2005 Philippine Star article says it was renamed in honor of a Filipino guerrilla who raised a flag on the summit during World War II.

This place is tied to the reason Siquijor is called the "island of healing" and the "mystical island." The island is said to have about 300 traditional healers, known as mananambal, and many of the herbs and trees they use come from this mountain. A 2014–2019 study recorded up to 218 plant species used by healers, and a 2019 plant survey identified 188 species in the forest, 19 of them threatened. Every Holy Week, the "Pahi-uli" Siquijor Healing Festival is held at the foot of the mountain.
For travelers it is an easy half-day trip. The road goes up almost to the summit, so after riding up by motorbike or tricycle you walk a staircase for about
10–20 minutes
to reach the viewing tower, about

high, and the viewing deck. On a clear day you can see the whole island coastline and Negros, and in very good weather Cebu and Bohol are said to be visible. On cloudy or foggy days you may not see even a few meters ahead, so keep your expectations modest. There are forest trails and facilities too. Along a concrete path through the forest run the 14 Stations of the Cross, and at the foot of the mountain there is a Lourdes grotto. On the northeast side of Mt. Bandilaan lies Cantabon Cave with its underground stream, and in Cang-apa village on the Larena side there is a butterfly garden; a loop combining them is known as the "mountain tour." Entry is generally described as free everywhere, but some reviews say a small donation or registration may be requested depending on management, so bring a little cash.
From the parking point just below the summit, a staircase leads up to a tower about

high. From the top you take in the whole island coastline in one view, and on clear days you can also see the mountain ridges of Negros. Some reviews mention worn railings, so check the condition before you climb.

Just before the summit there is a small park and a viewing platform facing east. Some travelers come for sunrise, but fog often settles in at dawn, and some guides say sunrise viewing is not permitted. Going around sunset to enjoy the cool breeze is also suggested.
The 14 stations run along a concrete path through the forest. A 2005 article says the staircase to the summit has
more than 300 steps
, and it is a path many pilgrims walk during Holy Week. You feel more of the forest than if you simply drive up and see only the summit.

This is the forest where mananambal gather herbs. It is said they collect on the seven Fridays before Holy Week, pruning branches rather than pulling plants out by the roots. Herb walking sections such as a "Healing Park" are sometimes mentioned along the road. It is good manners not to pick or dig up plants.

A 2005 article lists 27 bird species, more than 100 butterfly species, and trees such as narra, ipil and molave. The Siquijor bulbul (Hypsipetes siquijorensis), a species endemic to Siquijor, lives here, and the mountain is described as important habitat for it. You will often meet it by sound at dawn and in the early morning.
A small shrine at the foot of the mountain, visited by people praying for healing. It is not large, but it is a nice short stop on the way up the mountain road.

blocks.title: Cantabon Cave and the butterfly garden

children.text: Cantabon Cave on the northeast of the mountain is described as a route that follows an underground stream. The Siquijor Butterfly Garden in Cang-apa village on the Larena side is presented as a conservation project that breeds and releases butterflies. Check fees and opening hours locally.

items.title: Morning half-day course
items.subtitle: Viewing tower and the Stations of the Cross

children.text: Set out by scooter from Siquijor town or your lodging. Allowing for the time the fog lifts, we recommend heading up between
and
. There are no gas stations on the mountain road, so fill up before you leave.
At the entrance to the mountain road, check the signboard and information post, and register or donate if asked. The road is steep and rough in places, so go up slowly.
Reach the parking point below the summit and climb the staircase for about
10–20 minutes
. Go up the tower and look down over the whole island.
On the way down, walk part of the Stations of the Cross and the herb walking section, and have breakfast at the viewing platform.
Drop down to Cang-apa on the Larena side to see the butterfly garden, or head toward Cantabon Cave.
If time is tight, you can see only the tower and viewing deck and be back down within
2–3 hours

items.title: Full-day mountain tour
items.subtitle: Cave, butterfly garden and healers' villages

children.text: Explore the underground stream route at Cantabon Cave.
Drive up the summit road of Mt. Bandilaan and see the tower and viewing deck.
Have lunch and rest at a restaurant or village at the foot of the mountain.
Stop at the Cang-apa butterfly garden and a nearby waterfall.
The itinerary you agree on with a tricycle driver may change with local conditions, so settle the order and the fare before you set out.
There are direct flights from Manila to Dumaguete Sibulan Airport (DGT). From the airport, go to Dumaguete port and take a ferry bound for Siquijor.
From Cebu, fast crafts (for example OceanJet) are said to run from Cebu City port to Siquijor, but check travel time and fares in the operator's notices.
Siquijor Island itself has an airport, but scheduled flights change often, so check with the airline before you use it.
Ferry timetables change often with the weather and operator circumstances.
Because it is in the center of the island, it is described as about
30–50 minutes
from any port (Lazi about 30–40 minutes, Siquijor town about 40 minutes, Larena about 45 minutes, San Juan about 40–50 minutes).
Renting a scooter is the most convenient option. It is described as about ₱300~500 per day.
Tricycles and habal-habal (motorcycle taxis) can be found at San Fernando Park in Siquijor town, and a round-trip fare including waiting time needs to be bargained.
The mountain road can be slippery with fog and moss, so take care in the rainy season.
The dry season (November–May) is when the road is dry and visibility is good. Even so, the summit area is often foggy throughout the year, so a clear view is not guaranteed.
During Holy Week the healing festival and pilgrims make it crowded, but the atmosphere is special. To avoid the crowds, early on a weekday is best.

There is almost no accommodation on the mountain, so most people stay in Siquijor town, Lazi, or the San Juan beach area. A 2005 article mentions a DENR guesthouse offered free by advance request, but I could not confirm whether it operates now.

For meals, use restaurants in the villages at the foot of the mountain or small shops along the way. Some local guidance mentions limits on outside food, so bring only the water and snacks you need and take your trash with you.

The most common plan is to leave early from a beach lodging, see the mountain, and come back down to the sea in the afternoon. Rather than spending a night on the mountain, it is more realistic to stay at a beach resort in Lazi or San Juan and visit the mountain for half a day, and stopping at a waterfall or church on the way back fills out the day nicely.
Between
and
in the morning is best. Late in the afternoon it gets dark quickly because of the tall trees.
Opening hours differ by source, but many list
to
. Whether sunrise viewing is allowed differs by guide, so check locally.
Wear a helmet and ride a scooter slowly. There are no gas stations on the mountain.
Bring at least 1 liter of water, sturdy shoes, a light rain jacket, sunscreen, and a charged phone.
Do not pick or dig up plants in the forest. It is the herb forest the healers use.
During Holy Week the road is crowded with pilgrims and events, so leave plenty of time in your schedule.
Adding a cool highland half day between beach-focused days works well.
Ask permission before photographing local healers or residents, and remember that healing rituals are not a spectacle.
The road near the summit is steep and rough, and slippery with fog and moss. Do not go up on a rainy day or right after rain.
Some reviews say the tower's stairs and railings are worn, so check their condition before you use them.
Inexperienced scooter riders should go with a companion and tell their lodging their plans.
The forest paths are dense and you can lose your direction, so do not leave the marked trail.
Check the latest notices and local guidance for the entrance fee, opening hours, and whether sunrise viewing is allowed.
Mobile signal may be unreliable on the mountain, so download a map in advance.
A cave on the northeast side of Mt. Bandilaan that you walk along an underground stream. It is described as about
20–30 minutes
by car from the mountain, but check locally.
The island's signature waterfall, toward Lazi in the south. It is about
30–40 minutes
from the mountain and good for a swim.
A Spanish-era church and convent complex about
30–40 minutes
south of the mountain.
A small conservation facility in Cang-apa village on the Larena side. It is linked by the mountain road, so it combines well with the park.
